abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: The melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) is well‐established as a pivotal regulator of pigmentation in various species. Despite a wealth of research focused on mammals and fish, the role of Mc1r in amphibians has remained largely unexplored. This study was designed to elucidate the contribution of Mc1r in Xenopus tropicalis . Our results reveal that targeted ablation of mc1r in Xenopus tropicalis led to a significant reduction in dorsal skin pigmentation, while simultaneously accelerating the onset of melanophore pigmentation in the ventral region. This dual effect resulted in a perturbation of the canonical countershading pattern. Additionally, knockout of mc1r disrupted the expression of multiple genes primarily associated with pigmentation. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical role of MC1R in the regulation of pigmentation and the development of countershading in amphibians, contributing to the growing body of literature on the evolution and function of MC1R across vertebrate species.

list-item.p: The role of MC1R in dorsoventral pigmentation of Xenopus tropicalis is revealed for the first time.
In Xenopus tropicalis , mc1r knockout via CRISPR‐Cas9 significantly reduced dorsal pigmentation and advanced ventral melanophore appearance, disrupting the canonical countershading pattern.
Loss of mc1r alters the expression of multiple pigmentation‐related genes, highlighting its central role in the pigment regulatory network.
This study advances understanding of the conserved and divergent functions of MC1R in vertebrates, providing new insights into pigmentation regulation in amphibians and its evolutionary context.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Skin pigmentation is a vital phenotypic trait in vertebrates, serving roles in camouflage, UV protection, and social communication. It is influenced by genetic, environmental, and endocrine factors. In various animals, including fish, amphibians, and mammals, skin coloration is determined by the distribution, density, and activity of pigment cells such as melanophores (melanocytes in mammals), iridophores, and xanthophores. The regulation of pigment production and pigment cell behavior involves complex genetic and hormonal signaling pathways, with the MC1R being a key regulator of melanin synthesis and melanophore function (Stefania et al. 2024; Upadhyay et al. 2024; Yang 2011; Mun et al. 2023). MC1R is a seven‐transmembrane G protein‐coupled receptor primarily located on the surface of melanocytes. It features a conserved DRY (Asp‐Arg‐Tyr) motif at the junction of the third transmembrane domain, an N‐linked glycosylation site at the extracellular N‐terminus, and a palmitoylation site at the intracellular C‐terminus (Wenbo et al. 2025; Yang 2011). Encoded by the extension locus, MC1R's role in pigmentation was first identified in 1968 (Mountjoy et al. 1992; Robbins et al. 1993; Searle 1968). Activation of MC1R by its ligand, α‐melanocyte‐stimulating hormone (α‐MSH), stimulates eumelanin production, leading to darker pigmentation through the activation of intracellular cAMP/PKA signaling (Stefania et al. 2024; Upadhyay et al. 2024; Yang 2011; Mun et al. 2023).

Extensive studies in mammals, reptiles, and fish have demonstrated the essential role of MC1R/Mc1r in pigmentation, particularly in regulating melanin synthesis, including both eumelanin and pheomelanin (Alan et al. 2024; Stefania et al. 2024; Upadhyay et al. 2024; Yang 2011; Mun et al. 2023). Melanin is a versatile biopolymer present in various organisms, including animals, plants, fungi, and bacteria. Its diverse functions encompass photoprotection, pigmentation, antioxidant activity, thermoregulation, immune defense, and metal ion chelation (Graça and Michael S 2007; Jane et al. 2004; Liliana and Matthew D 2018; Slominski et al. 2022). Upon ultraviolet (UV) radiation, human and mouse keratinocytes upregulate POMC via the p53 pathway, producing α‐MSH (the cleavage product of POMC), which activates the cAMP/PKA/MITF/TYR signaling cascade in melanocytes to promote eumelanin synthesis (Böhm et al. 2025; Cui et al. 2007; Murase et al. 2009). This increases the eumelanin‐to‐pheomelanin ratio in melanocytes and facilitates eumelanin transfer to keratinocytes, protecting the skin from UV‐induced damage. Consequently, individuals with specific MC1R polymorphisms (e.g., red hair/fair skin, commonly known as RHC variants‐Red Hair Color) that impair eumelanin production are more susceptible to melanoma (Mitra et al. 2012; Sturm et al. 2003). Given its protective function, MC1R is considered a promising target for clinical therapies (Chen et al. 2017; Guida et al. 2022; Mun et al. 2023). Although UV radiation induces MC1R‐dependent melanin synthesis via the POMC‐derived peptide α‐MSH, hair follicle development and eumelanin deposition remain normal in the dorsal skin of Pomc
−/− mice (Slominski et al. 2005). This suggests that mouse MC1R may possess sufficient basal activity to sustain eumelanogenesis or that alternative non‐melanocortin pathways compensate for the absence of α‐MSH. Additionally, Mc1r regulates melanosome dispersion, contributing to adaptive background‐dependent color changes (Fujii 2000; Richardson et al. 2008). Moreover, MC1R, together with agouti signaling protein (ASIP), plays a pivotal role in countershading—a camouflage strategy characterized by a dark dorsal side and light ventral side. ASIP antagonizes α‐MSH by competitively binding MC1R, promoting pheomelanin synthesis and inhibiting melanocyte development (Aberdam et al. 1998; Bultman et al. 1992). Thus, asymmetric ASIP expression in the ventral region, along with MC1R activity, establishes countershading across species (Cal, Suarez‐Bregua, Braasch, et al. 2019; Cal, Suarez‐Bregua, Comesana, et al. 2019; Manceau et al. 2011; Vrieling et al. 1994). However, the specific function of Mc1r in amphibian pigmentation, particularly in Xenopus tropicalis , remains largely unexplored.

Xenopus tropicalis has emerged as a valuable model organism for developmental and genetic studies due to its diploid genome, short generation time, and well‐established genome editing tools (Carotenuto et al. 2023; El Mir et al. 2025; Ran, Li, Cheng, et al. 2024; Ran et al. 2022; Ran, Li, Xu, et al. 2024; Willsey et al. 2024; Yi et al. 2025). Despite its utility, the genetic mechanisms underlying skin pigmentation in Xenopus tropicalis have not been thoroughly investigated (El Mir et al. 2025; Liang et al. 2024; Yi et al. 2025). Understanding the function of pigmentation‐related genes like mc1r in this species could provide valuable insights into the evolutionary conservation and diversification of pigmentation pathways across vertebrates. In this study, we investigate the role of mc1r in Xenopus tropicalis by generating a loss‐of‐function mutation using CRISPR‐Cas9 genome editing. We examine how mc1r disruption affects melanophore distribution, melanin synthesis, and overall skin pigmentation during development. Our findings demonstrate that mc1r is essential for normal pigmentation in Xenopus tropicalis , expanding our understanding of pigment cell biology in vertebrates. These results not only enhance our understanding of amphibian pigmentation but also contribute to broader studies on the evolutionary genetics of coloration.

sec.title: Maintenance of Xenopus tropicalis
sec.p: In this study, Xenopus tropicalis were procured from Nasco (Fort Atkinson, WI, USA; http://www.enasco.com). The maintenance and husbandry of the frogs were conducted in accordance with established laboratory protocols (Ran, Li, Cheng, et al. 2024; Ran et al. 2022; Ran, Li, Xu, et al. 2024; Yi et al. 2025). Ethical approval for all animal experiments involving Xenopus tropicalis was granted by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Southern University of Science and Technology. The developmental stages of Xenopus tropicalis were classified using the staging criteria outlined by Nieuwkoop and Faber (Nieuwkoop and Faber 1994).

sec.title: CRISPR‐Cas9‐Mediated Gene Knockout and Efficiency Assessment
sec.p: To obtain gRNA (guide RNA), first, the pCS2‐SpCas9 plasmid was subjected to linearization using the restriction enzyme Not I and subsequently transcribed utilizing the mMessage mMachine SP6 Kit (Ambion, Austin, TX, USA). The target sequence for mc1r is 5′‐GGCCCCAAGAAAGGAGAGAGAGG‐3′. The gRNA template was synthesized through PCR amplification from the pUC57‐T7‐gRNA scaffold vector, employing a Trac‐reverse primer and a gRNA forward primer that included a T7 promoter sequence, the mc1r gRNA target sequence, and the scaffold sequence. Primer sequences are detailed in Table S1. In vitro transcription of the gRNA was facilitated by the Transcript Aid T7 High Yield Transcription Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Rockford, IL, USA). Cas9 mRNA and gRNA were purified using the RNeasy Mini Kit and miRNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), respectively.

For microinjection, the fertilized eggs of Xenopus tropicalis were collected via hormone‐induced mating, where adult male and female frogs were pre‐treated with 20 units of human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) 24 h prior, followed by a full dose of 145 units of HCG approximately 2–3 h before embryo collection. A mixture of Cas9 mRNA (300 pg per egg) and mc1r gRNA (200 pg per egg) was injected into fertilized eggs (2 nL per egg) from the animal pole.

To assess the efficiency of targeted mc1r disruption, genomic DNA was extracted from pooled healthy embryos 24 h post‐microinjection, and the targeted region was amplified by PCR. The purified PCR products were then cloned into the pMD18‐T vector (Takara, Katsu, Japan) using TA cloning. Randomly selected single colonies were subjected to Sanger DNA sequencing to detect indel (insertion or deletion) mutations. Mating of G0 frogs led to the production of homozygous mc1r disrupted frogs. Adult frogs were genotyped using small nail clippings, with genotyping PCR primer sequences provided in Table S1.

For odd‐target testing, potential off‐target sites were identified by mapping the mc1r gRNA target site to the Xenopus tropicalis genome (JGI 9.0) using CRISPOR, focusing on genomic loci with up to five mismatches relative to the mc1r gRNA coding sequence and following the NGG PAM sequence. Ten pairs of primers were designed for RT‐PCR amplification and subsequent Sanger DNA sequencing analysis based on the NCBI database, as listed in Table S1.

sec.title: Reverse Transcription‐Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT‐PCR)
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from embryos at various developmental stages and from distinct tissues harvested from adult Xenopus tropicalis using the TransZol Up Plus RNA Kit (Catalog Number: ER501‐01; Transgen Biotech, Beijing, China). Subsequently, reverse transcription was performed to generate a complementary DNA (cDNA) library, employing the TransScript Uni OneStep gDNA Removal and cDNA Synthesis SuperMix (Catalog Number: AU311‐03; Transgen Biotech, Beijing, China). The amplification of the gene of interest was achieved through polymerase chain reaction (PCR), utilizing primers whose sequences are detailed in Table S1. The relative expression levels of the transcripts were assessed by comparing the band intensities on agarose gels following gel electrophoresis.

sec.title: Whole Mount In Situ Hybridization (WISH)
sec.p: To elucidate the spatial and temporal expression patterns of specific genes during embryonic development, whole mount in situ hybridization (WISH) was conducted in accordance with methodologies previously described in the literature (Broadbent and Read 1999; Ran, Li, Xu, et al. 2024). Primer sequences utilized for the amplification of the target genes were detailed in Table S1.

sec.title: RNA Sequencing and Verification by Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
sec.p: Six wild‐type and six mc1r null adult frogs were picked randomly, and three replicates were set, including two frogs in each replicate. Total RNA extraction was the same as the method in RT‐PCR.

For RNA sequencing, mRNA was enriched by mRNA Capture Beads (Cat. N401‐02; Vazyme, Nanjing, China), and cDNA library was built through VAHTS Universal DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina V3 (Cat. ND607; Vazyme, Nanjing, China). The cDNA libraries were sent to Annoroad Gene Technology Company (Beijing, China) and sequenced. Transcriptome data were analyzed using our established protocol (Ran, Li, Cheng, et al. 2024; Yi et al. 2025). RNA‐seq data has been uploaded to the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) with the accession number PRJNA1256923.

In qPCR, some key genes in RNA sequencing analysis were selected to be verified, and the QuantiNova SYBR Green PCR Kit (Cat. 208056, QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany) was implemented as manipulation. The sequence of primers used in qPCR was listed in Table S1. Three technical replicates were set in every sample. The data was analyzed with Excel and visualized by GraphPad Prism 8.0.

sec.title: Protein–Protein Interaction (PPI) Network Analysis
sec.p: The list of genes was uploaded and analyzed in the online STRING tool (Szklarczyk et al. 2023). Given the scarcity of interaction data available for the species Xenopus tropicalis , we opted to utilize the Homo sapiens database as a surrogate for our analysis. The PPI result was visualized with Cytoscape software. The single nodes without edges were deleted in the picture.

sec.title: Transmission Electron Microscopy
sec.p: The skin was cut from frogs on ice. The sample was cut smaller than 1 × 1 mm, and then immersed in 2% glutaraldehyde in 1 × PBS as soon as possible, fixed overnight at 4°C. Then the sample was washed with 1 × PBS, and postfixed in 1% osmic acid at room temperature for 3 h, followed by washing with 1 × PBS and ddH2O. The skin was contrasted with 2% uranyl acetate overnight at 4°C, then washed with ddH2O at room temperature. Dehydration was implemented with acetone concentrated at 30% once, 50% once, 75% once, 100% twice, followed by embedding with acetone diluted epoxy resin concentrated at 25% once, 50% once, 75% once, and 100% twice. Then the sample was embedded in the box. Solidification was done at 65°C for 48 h. Ultrathin sectioning was done with an ultramicrotome (EM UC7; Leica, Wetzlar, Germany) and diamond knife (16DIA DU4530; Leica, Wetzlar, Germany). Sections were observed with an electron microscope (HT7700; Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan). Some samples were disposed of by Servicebio, Wuhan, China.

sec.title: Statistics and Reproducibility
sec.p: Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism version 9 (GraphPad Prism Software Inc., CA, USA) and expressed as means ± SD. Two‐way ANOVA was used to compare groups, with p < 0.05 considered significant. All experiments were replicated at least three times, and detailed methods are included in figure legends.

sec.title: Establishment of mc1r Null Xenopus tropicalis Line
sec.p: To establish an mc1r null Xenopus tropicalis line, we initially characterized the expression pattern of mc1r during embryonic development. RT‐PCR result showed that expression of mc1r began and dramatically increased between Stage 27–32, and increased along with development (Figure 1A). The result is consistent with RNA‐seq data obtained from Xenbase database (Bowes et al. 2010). In wild‐type tadpoles, the melanophores can be observed first at Stage 33/34. In tissues, mc1r were highly expressed in eye, dorsal skin, ventral skin where melanophores distributed (Figure 1B).

caption.p: Temporal expression pattern during tadpole development and spatial expression pattern in adult Xenopus tropicalis of mc1r through RT‐PCR. The result of RT‐PCR in (A) embryos at different stages and in (B) different organs of adult frog is shown. st, stage.

sec.p: In our RT‐PCR assays, we used equal amounts of total RNA for each reaction to ensure comparability between samples. However, we observed that the expression of gapdh, while commonly used as a loading control, is not uniform across different tissues in Xenopus tropicalis . This observation was consistent across repeated experiments and suggests tissue‐specific variation in gapdh expression at the mRNA level. Therefore, in this study, gapdh was not used for normalization. Instead, the results presented in Figure 1B reflect relative mc1r expression using equal RNA input across tissues. Notably, higher mc1r expression was detected in tissues rich in melanophores, such as the eye, dorsal skin, and ventral skin. This expression pattern supports the hypothesis that mc1r is involved in melanophore development and pigmentation.

As a GPCR protein, the DRY motif is conserved across various species, including Xenopus tropicalis Mc1r protein based on the homology analysis of protein sequence (Tai et al. 2022). Thus, we picked the upstream sequence of the DRY coding sequence as the SpCas9 knockout target for mc1r knockout (Figure 2). To detect the knockout efficiency in G0, PCR was done and the PCR product was inserted into a blunt plasmid followed by sequencing. Multiple insertions and deletions were created, and some of them were shown (Figure 2B). The efficiency of inducing mutations in G0 is 69.2% (9/13) (Table S2). To obtain the homozygote of the mc1r mutation, adult G0 frogs were crossed with adult wild‐type frogs to obtain the F1 generation; then, heterozygote F1 adult frogs were picked and crossed with each other to obtain the homozygote F2 generation. Through generation passage, the homozygotic mutants were obtained.

caption.p: mc1r knockout through CRISPR‐Cas9. (A) The target sequence is at nucleotide 6037–6059 in the mc1r gene indicated by an orange arrow head. The orange box indicates the exon, grey boxes indicate the untranslated regions (UTR) and the dotted line indicates the intron. (B) The sequence of the wild‐type target sequence (shown in orange) and some different insert/deletion (INDEL) situations in G0. bp, base pair (C) The mutated amino acid sequence led by a 4 bp deletion. TM, transmembrane; DRY, Asp‐Arg‐Tyr.

sec.title: mc1r Knockout Disturbs Melanophore Pattern in Xenopus tropicalis
sec.p: The phenotypes of different mc1r mutant lines are undistinguishable, thus we focus on one line, mc1r △4/△4 (Figure 2B,C), which is referred as mc1r null line in the following. With 4 bp deletion, the mutated Mc1r is predicted with a stop codon in advance (Figure 2C). Then two adult heterozygotic mc1r +/△4 frogs were picked and inbred. The pigment pattern of their offspring was observed and compared with wild‐type tadpoles. At first, the pigment pattern of these tadpoles was similar. Until Stage 43, two pigment patterns could be distinguished first time in the same batch through stereoscope observation (Figure 3A). The melanophores in some tadpoles became sparse both in head and trunk, while melanophores in others were dark and tight as wild‐type tadpoles. Tadpoles with normal or abnormal pigment pattern were picked to sequence the mc1r gene respectively. The genotype of tadpoles with abnormal pigment pattern was confirmed to mc1r null (about one quarter) while that of tadpoles with normal pigment pattern was wild‐type and heterozygous mc1r (about three quarters).

caption.p: mc1r knockout disturbs pigment pattern of post‐stage 43 tadpoles and frogs. (A) The tadpoles at stage 43, (B) the tadpoles at stage 52, (C) the tadpoles during metamorphosis at Stage 56–57, (D) the tadpoles at the end of metamorphosis at stage 59, (E) the froglets have finished metamorphosis, and (F) the adult frogs are shown in black boxes. The detailed pigment pattern marked with blue or orange boxes on tadpoles or frogs is shown in the boxes on right or bottom with corresponding colors respectively. The blue arrowheads indicate melanophores.

sec.p: Then when the tadpoles developed to about Stage 52, the mc1r null tadpoles looked much lighter than wild‐type tadpoles in dorsal view (Figure 3B). The melanophores on the surface of the brain and on the surface of some neurons or blood vessels observed in the mc1r null tadpoles were much fewer than in wild‐type tadpoles. There were few melanophores observed in the dorsal lateral skin in the head of mutants while there were groups of melanophores at the same location of wild‐type tadpoles. At this stage, few melanophores were observed in the ventral skin of both types of tadpoles.

When the tadpoles developed to metamorphotic stage (about Stage 55–58), the morphology of melanophores in the dorsal skin in wild‐type tadpoles and mutants was different (Figure 3C). In the head skin behind the nasals, there were two types of melanophores observed in wild‐type tadpoles, one looked much stronger, darker, and larger (indicated with I in Figure 3C) while another one looked much thinner and lighter (indicated with II in Figure 3C). Type I melanophores looked like flowers with many petals while type II melanophores looked like some thin strings. However, there were only type II melanophores that were thin and light observed in mutants at same location. Besides, in the lateral region of head skin, the melanophores of wild‐type tadpoles were also darker and larger than that in mutants. The melanophores in wild‐type tadpoles at this location were irregular dark dots with branches, while the branches of melanophores in mutants were hard to distinguish which made the melanophores look like round light dots at the same location.

Then at the end of metamorphosis (about Stage 59–62), there were more melanophores in dorsal skin, and they distributed much tightly in wild‐type tadpoles (Figure 3D). Surprisingly, there were melanophores observed already in the ventral skin of mc1r null tadpoles, while there were no melanophores observed in the ventral skin of wild‐type tadpoles at the same stage. Interestingly, this phenomenon lasted until the froglet stage that they had finished metamorphosis (Figure 3E). When there were melanophores scattered all over the ventral skin of mutants, there were few melanophores observed in the ventral skin of wild‐type froglets. This phenotype, which persists through metamorphosis and results in an atypical distribution of melanophores in post‐metamorphic froglets and adults, suggests a fundamental alteration in the spatiotemporal regulation of melanophore differentiation in the absence of mc1r. One possible explanation is that the Mc1r signaling pathway may act as a spatial regulator of melanophore development, not only promoting melanophore differentiation but also restricting their localization during development. In wild‐type tadpoles, the absence of melanophores in the ventral skin might reflect a tightly controlled spatial patterning mechanism that suppresses premature or ectopic melanophore differentiation in ventral regions. The loss of mc1r could impair this restriction, leading to a precocious and ectopic appearance of melanophores in the ventral skin. Furthermore, mc1r is known to be involved in melanocortin signaling, which can influence melanophore fate decisions and pigment production via cAMP‐mediated pathways (Stefania et al. 2024; Upadhyay et al. 2024; Mun et al. 2023). The disruption of this pathway may uncouple the usual dorsal–ventral gradients of melanophore‐inducing signals, leading to the derepression of melanophore differentiation in ventral regions. This finding contrasts with the delayed and denser accumulation of melanophores in dorsal skin of wild‐type animals, suggesting a complex, region‐specific regulation of pigment cell patterning that is perturbed in mc1r mutants. Future studies will be necessary to dissect the precise molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying this ventral‐specific phenotype, possibly by analyzing gene expression profiles of melanophore lineage cells along the dorsoventral axis in both wild‐type and mutant animals.

As they grow older, the skin of mutants looked much lighter than that of wild‐type frogs in dorsal view in the adult frogs, while the ventral skin looked a little darker than that of wild‐type frogs while there were high inter‐individual differences of ventral skin color between wild‐type frogs, some were darker while some were lighter (Figure 3F). In the dorsal skin, the melanophores in wild‐type frogs distributed tightly around the glands, intersected with each other, and it was difficult to count them. However, melanophores in the mutants distributed sparsely, more contracted, and it was easier to distinguish each other. The morphology of melanophores of ventral melanophores was similar in mutants and wild‐type frogs, which suggested that the differentiation of ventral melanophores was inhibited during metamorphosis and froglet stage, but the inhibition was partly released in following growth.

To conduct a numerical analysis of skin pigmentation, photographs were taken of equivalent dorsal and ventral regions from adult frogs. ImageJ software was then used to process the images. Due to the intersecting distribution of melanophores in wild‐type frogs, it was not feasible to count individual melanophores accurately. Instead, the ratio of pigmented areas relative to the total image area was quantified and analyzed (Figure 4A). The results indicated a significant reduction in dorsal pigmentation coverage in mc1r mutants compared to wild‐type controls. In contrast, the ratio of ventral pigmentation in wild‐type individuals exhibited considerable inter‐individual variation, making direct comparison inconclusive (Figure 4B).

caption.p: Numerical analysis shows the reduction of pigmentation in the dorsal skin of mc1r knockout frogs and the high inter‐individual variation in the ventral skin. (A) The method of numerical analysis. Photos are taken of equivalent dorsal and ventral regions from adult Xenopus tropicalis individuals. ImageJ is used to process the images. The ratio of pigmented areas relative to the total image area is quantified and analyzed. (B) Pigmentation ratio is compared among WT‐DS, mc1rKO‐DS, WT‐VS, and mc1rKO‐VS. DS, dorsal skin, VS, ventral skin.

sec.p: From the results above, it can be inferred that the development of melanophores is not disturbed by mc1r knockout at early stages (before Stage 43), but the amount and morphology of visible melanophores are disturbed along with growth. During metamorphosis, the onset of emergence of melanophores in ventral skin is in advance in mc1r mutants. In adult frogs, the dorsal skin of mc1r mutants is noticeably lighter in coloration compared to that of wild‐type individuals. In contrast, the ventral skin exhibits substantial inter‐individual variation, making reliable comparison difficult.

sec.title: The Development and Distribution of Melanoblasts in Embryonic Stages Are Not Disrupted by mc1r Knockout
sec.p: To test the development and distribution of melanoblasts in early developmental stages, whole mount in situ hybridization (WISH) was applied in embryos (Figure 5). Dopachrome tautomerase (dct) gene, premelanosome protein (pmel) gene, which are the markers of melanoblasts, and tyrosinase (tyr) gene, which is the marker of differentiating and differentiated melanophores were picked (Baxter and Pavan 2003; Mort et al. 2015). Five stages were picked from Stage 20 to 40. In both wild‐type and mc1r null embryos, there were melanoblast signals observed at Stage 20 with pmel and dct probes, while almost no signal was observed at this stage with the tyr probe. Then the melanophore signals were high in the eyes and dorsolateral region with pmel, dct, and tyr probes in embryos from Stage 26 to 40. There were no signals observed in the ventral region. The expression pattern in mc1r null tadpoles was similar to that in wild‐type tadpoles, suggesting that the loss of mc1r may not affect the initial formation and early differentiation of melanophore lineage cells. One possible explanation is that compensatory mechanisms may exist during early embryonic stages to maintain normal development of the melanophore lineage. For example, other members of the melanocortin receptor family, such as mc5r or mc4r, might partially compensate for the loss of mc1r signaling or regulate cAMP levels to support proper melanoblast differentiation. In addition, the early melanophore lineage may rely more on coordinated regulation by other factors such as mitf, sox10, and foxd3, rather than solely depending on mc1r signaling, which could explain the absence of an observable phenotype at this stage (Alessandro and Elizabeth 2024; Steel et al. 1992). Furthermore, we observed that although there were no significant differences in differentiation signals and distribution patterns during early development, regional changes in melanophore distribution emerged during later metamorphic stages. This suggests that the regulatory role of mc1r may be more prominent in later stages of development, particularly in fine‐tuning processes such as melanophore migration, spatial distribution, or pigment deposition, rather than in the initial establishment of the melanophore lineage.

caption.p: Whole mount in situ hybridization result of pmel, dct, and tyr in wild‐type and mc1r null tadpoles at different stages is shown.

sec.title: mc1r Knockout Disturbed Expression of Multiple Pigmentation‐Related Genes in Skin of Adult Xenopus tropicalis
sec.p: Next, we tested the differentiated gene expression disturbed by mc1r knockout in adult frogs, both in dorsal skin and ventral skin. RNA sequencing was implemented, and the differentiated expression genes (DEGs) were filtered. The results showed that there were 315 genes up‐regulated and 95 genes down‐regulated in dorsal skin (DS), while 336 genes up‐regulated and 98 genes down‐regulated in ventral skin (VS) because of mc1r knockout. Six essential melanophore‐related genes were picked (tyrp1, tyr, slc24a5, pmel, mlana, dct) to analyze both in DS and VS (Figure 6A). Specifically, Tyr (tyrosinase) is the rate‐limiting enzyme in melanin biosynthesis, catalyzing the initial steps of tyrosine conversion to DOPA and dopaquinone (Liliana and Matthew D 2018). Tyrp1 and Dct (also known as Tyrp2) act downstream in the pathway, modulating the type of melanin produced (Liliana and Matthew D 2018). Pmel encodes a structural protein essential for the formation of melanosomal fibrils, serving as a scaffold for melanin deposition (Liliana and Matthew D 2018). Mlana (Melan‐A) is involved in melanosome maturation and cooperates with Pmel (Liliana and Matthew D 2018). Slc24a5 encodes a sodium/potassium/calcium exchanger protein that helps maintain ion balance within melanosomes and influences pigmentation (Ellen E and Mark D 2008). The expression levels of these genes serve as indicators of melanophore differentiation status and melanin production activity. Therefore, we analyzed their expression patterns in both DS and VS to further understand the effects of mc1r knockout on melanophore distribution and function.

caption.p: The differentiated expression genes related with melanophores are analyzed by RNA‐seq and verified by qPCR. (A) The essential genes related with melanophore are selected and analyzed based on the RNA‐seq result. The blue dots indicate the genes are downregulated while the pink dots mean the genes are not disturbed obviously. (B) Three essential melanophore related genes downregulated in DS analyzed by RNA‐seq (tyr, dct, and pmel) are selected and tested by qPCR, accorded with RNA‐seq result.

sec.p: Data analysis showed that all of them were downregulated in DS with extremely low p‐value (high reliability), while there was no obvious disturbance led by mc1r knockout in VS with relatively high p‐value (low reliability) (Table S3). The data showed that the expression level of these genes in ventral skin among different wild‐type frogs was highly variable, which inferred that the mechanisms regulating the ventral skin color were complicated, leading to such high inter‐individual difference. The result was accorded with observations in adult frogs as mentioned above. Following RNA‐seq, qPCR was applied to verify the result. The expression level of three key melanophore‐related genes tyr, pmel, and dct was tested in dorsal skin (Figure 6B). All of them were downregulated accorded with the RNA‐seq result. Thus, it could be concluded that mc1r knockout decreased the expression level of melanophore‐related genes in dorsal skin of adult frogs, leading to lighter skin color observed from the top.

Then, the intersected genes that up‐/down‐regulated in both DS and VS were filtered (Table S4). The GO enrichment and KEGG pathway enrichment of 179 upregulated genes together with 26 downregulated genes with clear gene names were analyzed with DAVID tool (Figure 7, Table 1). Firstly, the GO‐BP (biological process) result (Figure 7A) showed that 20 genes were enriched in phosphorylation, while phosphorylation is essential in signal transduction of mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway (Peterson et al. 2022), an important pathway in melanin synthesis (D'Mello et al. 2016). Among the list, Map3k15 (MAPK/ERK Kinase Kinase 15) and Map4k1 (MAPK/ERK Kinase Kinase Kinase 1) translated by map3k15, map4k1 are the upstream kinases of MAPK signaling. It could be inferred that MAPK signaling might be disturbed in mc1r mutants. Secondly, the GO‐CC result (Figure 7B) showed that most of the proteins translated by disturbed genes were in the cytoplasm. Thirdly, in GO‐MF analysis (Figure 7C), 26 genes were enriched in ATP binding function. Whether this result was led by cAMP signaling pathway disturbance still needed further research. Besides, 9 genes were enriched in DNA binding function. Based on GeneCards database, their differentiated expression might disturb immune response, circadian clock, and cellular growth and differentiation. Finally, in KEGG pathway result (Figure 7D), 9 genes were enriched in endocytosis. Based on GeneCards database, they might be related to vesicular transport, endosome and lysosome, protein trafficking, and so on. So, their disturbance might affect melanosome formation and transport directly or indirectly. Interestingly, the genes cldn17.1 and cldn17.3 which encode a tight junction protein Claudin17 were highly upregulated both in dorsal skin and ventral skin in our RNA‐seq data. Claudin17 forms tight junction channels with distinct anion selectivity in claudin family (Conrad et al. 2016; Krug et al. 2012). The route from Mc1r to cldn17 gene expression, and the effect led by increased cldn17 gene expression level still needed further research.

sec.p: At the same time, the protein–protein interaction (PPI) was analyzed with the STRING database and visualized with Cytoscape software (Figure 8). Due to the limited availability of PPI data for Xenopus tropicalis , the human ( Homo sapiens ) PPI database was employed in this study. The results revealed that SRC occupies a central node within the network, interacting with numerous proteins. Besides, CD3G, CD247, NR1D1, CCL5, and GRAP2 are associated with relatively fewer proteins, forming smaller regulatory hubs. Additionally, proteins such as PER3, SKAP1, PER1, LAT, MAP4K1, CXCL10, and IRF1 were found to interact with a limited number of neighboring proteins, forming localized regulatory networks. The PPI analysis suggests that mc1r knockout may disrupt the normal physiological activity of melanophores and surrounding tissues by interfering with these protein regulatory networks. These proteins may themselves act either as downstream targets affected by other factors or as upstream regulators influencing other proteins (i.e., cause or result).

caption.p: STRING analysis of PPI (protein–protein interaction) and visualized by Cytoscape. Darker color means higher degree.

sec.title: The Ultrastructure of Melanosome Is Not Disrupted by mc1r Knockout
sec.p: Further, the ultrastructure of melanosomes was tested under transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The MC1R gene is known to regulate the synthesis of eumelanin and pheomelanin, while previous studies have reported that eumelanin and pheomelanin display distinct ultrastructural characteristics under TEM (Slominski et al. 2004). Therefore, it is worthwhile to investigate whether melanin synthesis is affected in Xenopus tropicalis mc1r mutants.

TEM is available for analyzing organelles in chromatophores, and it is the gold standard of chromatophore determination. The chromatophores can be distinguished based on their specific organelles: melanophores have melanosomes, which are black ovals (Figure 9B, “M”), xanthophores have pterinosomes, which are spherical with some internal concentric lamellae (Figure 9B, “X”), and iridophores have reflecting platelets, which are elongated hollows (Figure 9B, “I”) (Bagnara et al. 1968). They distribute in the dermis layer under the basal membrane. The ultrastructure of melanosomes in Xenopus tropicalis melanophores is distinctive compared with that in mammals (Slominski et al. 2004), while melanosomes in Xenopus tropicalis are more amorphous than in mammals. In the dorsal skin of froglets (Figure 9A), both wild‐type and mc1r null melanophores were filled with vacuoles, each containing a black oval in the center with some little dots around the oval. In adult frogs (Figure 9B), the distribution and ultrastructure of chromatophores of mc1r null frogs in dorsal skin were not disrupted compared with those of wild‐type frogs. In a magnified view, both amorphous ovals and regular ellipses can be observed in wild‐type and mc1r null melanosomes in adult frogs (Figure 9C). Based on the undiscernible ultrastructure of melanosome, it can be inferred that the melanin type synthesized in Xenopus tropicalis is not disrupted by mc1r knockout. However, the quantity and the ratio of pheomelanin and eumelanin still need further measurement through other physicochemical methods.

caption.p: Transmission electron microscopy result is shown. (A) The ultrastructure of melanophores in wild‐type and mc1r null froglets (×8k). (B) The overall chromatophore distribution under basal membrane (×1k) and (C) ultrastructure of melanosomes (×12k) in wild‐type and mc1r null adult frogs. BM, basal membrane; I, iridophore; M, melanophore; X, xanthophore. Black arrowheads indicate melanosomes.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, mc1r was knocked out using CRISPR‐Cas9 in Xenopus tropicalis . Prior to metamorphosis, mc1r‐null tadpoles exhibited fewer dorsal melanophores than wild‐type, with minimal ventral pigmentation in both. Wild‐type tadpoles displayed two melanophore morphologies—dense, dark cells and sparse, lighter ones—whereas only the latter was seen in mutants. By metamorphosis completion, melanophores appeared in the ventral skin of mc1r‐null tadpoles earlier than in wild‐type, a difference that persisted into the froglet stage. In adulthood, despite similar melanosome ultrastructure between groups, mc1r‐null frogs showed visibly lighter dorsal skin and earlier, more extensive ventral pigmentation, disrupting the typical countershading pattern.

Notably, the early appearance of melanophores in the ventral skin of mc1r‐null tadpoles was unexpected and persisted through metamorphosis, eventually leading to an aberrant melanophore distribution in froglets and adult frogs. This observation suggests that loss of mc1r may fundamentally alter the spatiotemporal regulation of melanophore differentiation. A possible explanation for this phenotype is that mc1r signaling may not only promote melanophore differentiation but also restrict their spatial distribution during development. In wild‐type animals, the absence of melanophores in the ventral skin during early stages may reflect a tightly regulated patterning mechanism that prevents premature or ectopic melanophore differentiation. In contrast, mc1r deletion may disrupt this regulation, resulting in premature and ectopic melanophore development in the ventral region. This is further supported by our observation that only the lighter, loosely distributed melanophore type was present in mc1r‐null tadpoles, while wild‐type tadpoles exhibited both light and dark melanophores. Previous studies have shown that mc1r mediates melanocortin signaling via a cAMP‐dependent pathway, which governs both pigment production and cell fate decisions in melanophores (Alan et al. 2024; Alessandro and Elizabeth 2024; Böhm et al. 2025; Stefania et al. 2024; Upadhyay et al. 2024; Wenbo et al. 2025; Mun et al. 2023). Disruption of this pathway may interfere with the dorsal‐ventral gradient of melanogenic signals, effectively removing inhibitory cues that restrict ventral melanophore differentiation. This leads to a reversal or loss of the typical countershading pattern, where pigmentation is normally denser dorsally and reduced ventrally. Despite the similar melanosome ultrastructure observed in adult mc1r‐null and wild‐type frogs, the dorsal skin of mutants appeared significantly lighter. This discrepancy suggests that mc1r also regulates melanophore morphology or pigment content beyond early differentiation. Taken together, our findings reveal a novel role for mc1r in the spatial patterning of melanophores along the dorsal‐ventral axis and highlight metamorphosis as a critical window for pigment pattern establishment. Future studies should explore the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms—such as the spatial expression profiles of melanophore lineage genes—to further dissect how mc1r influences regional melanophore development and patterning in Xenopus tropicalis . Moreover, due to its extended metamorphic period, Xenopus tropicalis offers a longer window to observe pigment pattern establishment than zebrafish, making it an ideal model for future research.
In conclusion, mc1r knockout alters melanophore distribution and morphology post‐stage 43, advancing ventral pigmentation onset and disrupting normal countershading in Xenopus tropicalis .
